---
title: Peer-Feedback Seminar
---

## Task

Provide feedback on the draft of your assigned peer. 

### Seminar Instructions

Structure your feedback as a reader who does not get paid to read the text: "as a reader, I got lost here / didn't believe this / wanted to know Y / really enjoyed X".

#### Argument

- State the authors central claim back to them, see if it matches what they thought their central argument was 

#### Course engagement


- Which concepts from the course are central to the essay? How precisely are they used?

- Is anything from the course missing that would strengthen the argument?

#### Theories and evidence


- Are these concepts load-bearing, in other words, would the argument fall apart without them?

- How is evidence used in the essay? Where is it the thinnest relative to the weight it carries in the argument? Is it well sourced and motivated?
  
#### Reader Experience

- Mark the place you got lost, bored, or skeptical.
- Mark the place you were most convinced or interested.

#### Anthology readiness

- Would a reader outside this course follow the argument?
- Is there a sentence or paragraph you'd want to quote? (Useful positive signal.)

During the seminar you will get five minutes to deliver your feedback. Note that this is not a defense, just an opportunity to improve your essay. If we have time left we will get started with making plans for improvements.

## Helpful resources on writing

This video by the [University of Chicago Leadership Lab: The Craft of Writing Effectively](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vtIzMaLkCaM)is aimed at doctoral students or early career researchers, but it holds a lot of value for any scientific writing. I highly recommend watching it over and over again.

[Our library services](https://www.lunduniversity.lu.se/current-students/student-services-and-support/support-study-skills-language-and-academic-writing/academic-support-centre) have a lot of resources for student's writing---use them!
